idiom_name: one link table per association, written by exactly one owning mapper
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: create one table for the association with two foreign keys — one per end — and a composite primary key (not merely a unique index) over the pair so the same link cannot exist twice and the DB enforces uniqueness without a convention. Declare both foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE (or delete the link rows explicitly before deleting an end) so no row can reference a missing object. Name exactly one side as the owner of the association: its mapper inserts a row when the collection gains an element and deletes the row when it loses one; the other side only reads. Read collections with a single join or one batched query for all ids in hand, never per object. For the non-owning side index: a single composite index on (second_fk, first_fk) is sufficient for both directions in PostgreSQL — do not create redundant mirror indexes. Leave a migration path open: the day the link needs attributes, map the table as an entity and replace the collection with two one-to-many relationships. Prefer Set over List in language runtimes that support both: Set semantics allow the ORM to generate targeted INSERT/DELETE rather than delete-all-reinsert.
pitfalls: Putting link-row management on both sides: two writers insert the same pair, and only the composite key stands between you and duplicates.
Omitting the composite key or unique index: the collections look deduplicated in memory while the table accumulates repeated links.
Loading the collection per object in a loop — the association's join is cheap, doing it N times is not.
Forgetting cascade or explicit link deletion, so deletions leave rows pointing at objects that no longer exist.

Using a List instead of a Set for the in-memory collection: the ORM cannot determine which specific elements changed and issues DELETE ALL + INSERT ALL for every collection mutation, producing O(N) SQL for a one-element change.
Missing or incorrect equals()/hashCode() on entity classes used in a Set-backed collection: two loaded instances of the same entity are treated as distinct, causing duplicate-key violations.
Bidirectional ORM collections that are not kept in sync: adding to the owning side but not the inverse side leaves the in-memory model stale.
Using FetchType.EAGER on a mapped collection, loading the entire association set on every parent query — the single most common cause of Hibernate/SQLAlchemy OOM kills in production.
JOIN FETCH on two List-backed collections in one query: Hibernate throws MultipleBagFetchException; the Cartesian product multiplies result-set rows.
CascadeType.REMOVE or CascadeType.ALL on @ManyToMany: propagates deletion to the associated entity itself, removing shared records that other parents still reference.
Letting both navigable sides write the link: concurrent updates produce duplicate-key errors (or duplicate rows without a constraint) -> designate one owning writer and enforce the composite key.

Keeping quantity, rank, or status in an implicit collection mapping: the payload has no stable home and link-specific reports cannot address it -> promote the table to an association entity with two one-to-many relationships.

Wrong move: mutate a many-to-many collection only on the inverse (mappedBy) side -> failure: JPA and Hibernate flush silently without writing the link row, so the association looks saved in memory and missing after reload -> instead: write through the owning side and keep both views in sync with utility methods.

Wrong move: rely on a bare join table that cannot carry attributes because the schema happens to allow it (Rails has_and_belongs_to_many, Hibernate unidirectional @ManyToMany) -> failure: the first role, quantity, or timestamp forces a migration and rewrites every query that used the implicit form -> instead: start with the explicit join model (has_many :through, association entity) unless the pair is provably permanent.

Wrong move: attach and detach link rows in a loop over an existing association set -> failure: each call is a round trip and concurrent attach racing a full delete-all resynchronisation (Laravel sync, JPA remove-all/insert-all on a List) duplicates or resurrects rows -> instead: diff the desired pair set against current rows and issue targeted INSERT/DELETE, or a single set-based sync inside one transaction.
Walking every parent and touching its lazy collection: the ORM emits N+1 queries and can load an unbounded set -> batch by owner ids or page/query the link table directly.
